Abstract
                Background
                Deep mutational scanning (DMS) studies exploit the mutational landscape of sequence variation by systematically and comprehensively assaying the effect of single amino acid variants (SAVs; also referred to as missense mutations, or non-synonymous Single Nucleotide Variants – missense SNVs or nsSNVs) for particular proteins. We assembled SAV annotations from 22 different DMS experiments and normalized the effect scores to evaluate variant effect prediction methods. Three trained on traditional variant effect data (PolyPhen-2, SIFT, SNAP2), a regression method optimized on DMS data (Envision), and a naïve prediction using conservation information from homologs.
              
                Results
                On a set of 32,981 SAVs, all methods captured some aspects of the experimental effect scores, albeit not the same. Traditional methods such as SNAP2 correlated slightly more with measurements and better classified binary states (effect or neutral). Envision appeared to better estimate the precise degree of effect. Most surprising was that the simple naïve conservation approach using PSI-BLAST in many cases outperformed other methods. All methods captured beneficial effects (gain-of-function) significantly worse than deleterious (loss-of-function). For the few proteins with multiple independent experimental measurements, experiments differed substantially, but agreed more with each other than with predictions.
              
                Conclusions
                DMS provides a new powerful experimental means of understanding the dynamics of the protein sequence space. As always, promising new beginnings have to overcome challenges. While our results demonstrated that DMS will be crucial to improve variant effect prediction methods, data diversity hindered simplification and generalization.

Abstract

Background
Deep mutational scanning (DMS) investigates the mutational landscape of sequence variation by systematically and comprehensively measuring how single amino acid variants (SAVs; also called missense mutations, or non-synonymous Single Nucleotide Variants—missense SNVs or nsSNVs) affect specific proteins. We compiled SAV annotations from 22 DMS experiments and normalized the effect scores to assess variant effect prediction methods. We evaluated three methods trained on conventional variant effect data (PolyPhen-2, SIFT, SNAP2), a regression approach optimized for DMS data (Envision), and a naïve predictor based on conservation information from homologs.

Results
Across 32,981 SAVs, all methods captured some features of the experimental effect scores, though not the same ones. Conventional methods such as SNAP2 showed slightly higher correlation with measurements and performed better at binary classification of effect versus neutral states. Envision seemed to estimate the exact magnitude of effect more accurately. Most notably, the simple naïve conservation method using PSI-BLAST outperformed the other methods in many cases. All methods detected beneficial effects (gain-of-function) much less well than deleterious effects (loss-of-function). For the few proteins with multiple independent experimental measurements, the experiments varied substantially, but they agreed with one another more than with the predictions.

Conclusions
DMS offers a powerful new experimental way to study the dynamics of protein sequence space. As always, promising beginnings must still overcome challenges. Our results show that DMS will be essential for improving variant effect prediction methods, but data diversity limited simplification and generalization.
